facts.statement: Wannchampsus is an extinct genus of neosuchian closely related to but distinct from true crocodilians.
facts.quote: Wannchampsus ("Wann Langston, Jr.'s crocodile") is an extinct genus of paralligatorid neosuchian, close to but not a true crocodilian.

facts.statement: Fossils of Wannchampsus have been found in Lower Cretaceous rocks in north-central Texas, United States.
facts.quote: It is known from fossils discovered in Lower Cretaceous rocks in north-central Texas, United States.

facts.statement: The genus Wannchampsus was described by Thomas Adams in 2014.
facts.quote: Wannchampsus was described in 2014 by Thomas Adams.

facts.statement: The type species W. kirpachi was named in honor of Wesley Kirpach for his role in discovering and excavating the type specimen.
facts.quote: The type species is W. kirpachi, in honor of Wesley Kirpach, "who was instrumental in the discovery and excavations of the type specimen".

facts.statement: The genus Wannchampsus is based on the partial skull and lower jaw fossil SMU 76604.
facts.quote: Wannchampsus is based on SMU 76604, a partial skull and lower jaw.

facts.statement: Associated fossils found with the main specimen mostly consist of forelimbs and vertebrae.
facts.quote: A handful of other fossils were found associated, mostly representing forelimbs and vertebrae.

facts.statement: Fossils were found in the late Aptian-age Lower Cretaceous Twin Mountains Formation near Stephenville, Texas, at a site known as the Proctor Lake dinosaur locality.
facts.quote: These fossils were found in rocks of the late Aptian-age Lower Cretaceous Twin Mountains Formation, southwest of Stephenville, in Comanche County, Texas; the site is otherwise known as the Proctor Lake dinosaur locality.

facts.statement: The skulls of Wannchampsus are described as low, broad, and small, with the largest specimen estimated at 64 mm in length.
facts.quote: The skulls are described as "low and broad", and are small; SMU 76604 is estimated at 64 mm long, and SMU 76605 is estimated at 62 mm long.

facts.statement: Features of the skull and vertebrae suggest that the known individuals were subadults.
facts.quote: Features of the skull and vertebrae indicate that the individuals are subadults.

facts.statement: Wannchampsus is classified within the family Paralligatoridae.
Wannchampsus lived during the Aptian to Albian stages, between 119.57 and 110.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Albian (119.57 to 110.1 million years ago)
